modules.title: Python Core, Idioms & OOP
modules.why: Every later phase is written in Python; fluency here compounds into everything from data work to agent orchestration.
objectives: Use exceptions, context managers, and pathlib
Read and debug unfamiliar Python quickly
completion: Solve 30 varied exercises without a JS-to-Python mental translation
Explain decorators and generators with an example of each
Type-annotate a 200-line module and pass mypy --strict
modules.deliverable: A small typed Python library (e.g. a CLI expense tracker) with docstrings and tests.

modules.title: Environments, Modules & Dependencies
modules.why: Virtual environments and packaging are the difference between "works on my machine" and reproducible AI projects.
objectives: Pin dependencies and understand lock files
Publish or install an editable package
completion: Install your Phase-1 library into a fresh venv from a lock file
Explain why installing globally is a trap
modules.deliverable: Your tracker library installed as a package with pinned, reproducible dependencies.

modules.title: NumPy, pandas & Visualisation
modules.why: The lingua franca of ML data preparation; also your bridge from the Netflix/sentiment projects to rigorous pipelines.
objectives: Clean, join, group, and reshape data with pandas
completion: Rewrite a slow loop as vectorised NumPy and benchmark the speedup
Produce an exploratory data analysis notebook on a messy real dataset
modules.deliverable: An EDA notebook (with narrative) on a public dataset, exported to HTML.

modules.title: HTTP, JSON, APIs & Async Python
modules.why: LLM apps are network programs: async API calls, streaming responses, and retries are the daily bread of AI engineering.
objectives: Call REST APIs with requests and httpx
Understand status codes, headers, auth, pagination
Write async coroutines and gather concurrent calls
Handle errors, timeouts, and exponential backoff
completion: Fetch from 3 paginated public APIs concurrently with retries
Explain when async beats threads and when it does not
modules.deliverable: A resilient API client module with tests using recorded responses.

modules.title: Git, GitHub, Testing & Clean Code
modules.why: Employers read your Git history and run your tests; both are part of proving engineering ability.
completion: Get a PR reviewed and merged into your own project
Reach high coverage on the API client module
modules.deliverable: A public repo with CI running tests on every push.

modules.title: SQL & Database Basics
modules.why: Conversation state, user data, and production persistence all live in databases you must be able to query directly.
objectives: Use SQLite and Postgres from Python
Understand transactions at a basic level
completion: Write 20 queries including multi-table joins and aggregates
Design a schema for a chat application with conversation history
modules.deliverable: A normalised SQLite schema plus a query cheat-sheet you wrote yourself.

modules.title: Checkpoint Project: API Insight Tracker
modules.why: Proves Phase 1 end-to-end: real API, persistence, tests, packaging — the template for every future project.
objectives: Consume a public API on a schedule
Surface insight via CLI or tiny web page
completion: Deployed or runnable by a stranger in under 5 minutes from your README
modules.deliverable: Portfolio project #1 (see Projects page).

modules.title: Linear Algebra for ML
modules.why: Embeddings, attention, and every model weight are vectors and matrices; this module makes them geometric and intuitive.
objectives: Vectors, dot products, and cosine similarity by hand
completion: Compute dot products and cosine similarity without reference
Explain what a matrix multiplication does geometrically
modules.deliverable: A Jupyter notebook deriving and visualising each concept with tiny numerical examples.

modules.title: Probability & Statistics
modules.why: Evaluation is statistics. Precision/recall, confidence, and distributions decide whether your AI system actually works.
objectives: Sampling and the central limit theorem
completion: Solve base-rate problems correctly (see the diagnostic!)
Explain what a confidence interval does and does not mean
modules.deliverable: A notebook applying Bayesian reasoning to a real spam/medical-style screening example.

modules.title: Calculus Essentials & Gradients
modules.why: Training any neural network is gradient descent; you need just enough calculus to own that idea.
objectives: Gradient descent by hand and in NumPy
completion: Fit a line to points with hand-written gradient descent
Explain the chain rule with a two-layer example
modules.deliverable: Gradient-descent-from-scratch notebook with visualised loss curves.

modules.title: Supervised & Unsupervised Learning
modules.why: Classical ML teaches methodology (splits, baselines, metrics) that agent evaluation inherits wholesale.
completion: Build a baseline-first pipeline and beat it deliberately
Choose metrics justified by class balance and costs
modules.deliverable: A trained, evaluated model notebook with honest error analysis.

modules.title: Preprocessing, Overfitting & Evaluation
modules.why: The gap between tutorial ML and defensible ML: leakage, proper cross-validation, and metric choices you can justify.
objectives: Encodings, scaling, and pipelines that avoid leakage
completion: Find and fix a deliberately planted leakage bug
Defend your metric choice for an imbalanced problem
modules.deliverable: A leakage-hunt write-up plus corrected pipeline.

modules.title: Experiment Tracking & Reproducibility
modules.why: Optional but high-leverage: tracking turns flailing into science and directly transfers to LLM evaluation later.
completion: Reproduce any past run from its record alone
modules.deliverable: A tracked experiment table for your Phase-2 project.

modules.title: Checkpoint Project: Rigorous ML App
modules.why: Rebuild your sentiment project with proper methodology — the perfect "I leveled up" portfolio story.
completion: A reviewer can reproduce your headline number
modules.deliverable: Portfolio project #2 (see Projects page).

modules.title: Neural Networks & Backpropagation
modules.why: Owning backprop demystifies everything later — training, fine-tuning, and why agents cost tokens.
objectives: Backprop by hand on a tiny network
completion: Train an MLP on MNIST in pure NumPy
Explain vanishing gradients and one fix
modules.deliverable: From-scratch NumPy neural network notebook.

modules.title: PyTorch Fundamentals
modules.why: PyTorch is the research-and-industry default; every open-weight model you will touch is a PyTorch model.
completion: Rewrite your NumPy network in PyTorch and match accuracy
Fine-tune a pretrained image classifier on new classes
modules.deliverable: A PyTorch training repo with config-driven runs.

modules.title: Embeddings & Representation Learning
modules.why: The single most reused idea in applied AI: meaning as geometry powers search, RAG, and memory.
objectives: Train a small embedding model (e.g. word2vec-style)
completion: Explain why cosine beats Euclidean for text
Build a semantic search over 100 sentences
modules.deliverable: Interactive similarity notebook + short write-up.

modules.title: Attention & the Transformer
modules.why: The transformer is the machine inside every LLM; understanding Q/K/V removes the magic from the whole field.
objectives: Trace one forward pass on paper
completion: Implement single-head attention in ~30 lines
Explain why attention scales quadratically with sequence length
modules.deliverable: Annotated mini-transformer implementation (Karpathy-style).

modules.title: Tokenisation, Context Windows & Inference
modules.why: Tokens are the unit of cost, latency, and memory in every LLM system you will engineer.
objectives: KV cache and why inference is fast
completion: Predict which strings tokenise expensively
Explain the KV cache to a colleague
modules.deliverable: Token-cost analysis of real prompts using tiktoken.

modules.title: Pretraining, Fine-tuning & Inference Optimisation
modules.why: Optional specialisation: needed for LLM-engineer research-flavoured roles; awareness suffices for most agent roles.
objectives: When fine-tuning is the wrong answer
completion: LoRA-fine-tune a small open model on a toy task
Run a quantised model locally and measure quality/speed
modules.deliverable: Fine-tuning experiment report with before/after evals.

modules.title: Checkpoint Project: Neural Net + Pretrained Models
modules.why: Consolidates Phase 3: your own tiny network plus confident use of pretrained models.
objectives: Train and evaluate your own model
completion: Written comparison with numbers, not vibes
modules.deliverable: Model comparison write-up in your portfolio repo.

modules.title: LLM APIs & Local Open-Weight Models
modules.why: First contact with the raw material of agent engineering — and motivation fuel: you can start here early.
completion: Same prompt across cloud and local models, compared
Explain temperature and when you want it near zero
modules.deliverable: A tiny provider-independent wrapper module with tests.

modules.title: Prompt Design, System Instructions & Context
modules.why: Prompts are programs with fuzzy semantics; engineering them (and versioning them) is a core job skill.
completion: Improve a weak prompt measurably on 20 test cases
Explain why prompts must be treated as code under test
modules.deliverable: A prompt library repo with before/after eval cases.

modules.title: Structured Outputs & Schema Validation
modules.why: Agents that emit sloppy JSON break pipelines; validated schemas are what make LLM output programmable.
objectives: Validation failure handling and repair loops
completion: Zero invalid outputs across 200 sampled generations
Implement a validate-and-retry loop with error feedback
modules.deliverable: A typed output layer reused by your Phase-4 project.

modules.title: Function Calling & Tool Use
modules.why: The exact mechanism behind every agent: the model requests actions, your code executes them.
objectives: Define tool schemas the model can use
Design tool descriptions that get picked correctly
completion: Build a 3-tool assistant with correct tool selection on 30 test prompts
modules.deliverable: Tool-using assistant core with fixtures-based tests.

modules.title: Streaming, Retries, Rate Limits & Errors
modules.why: Production LLM apps fail at the network and budget layer far more than at the prompt layer.
completion: Survive a chaos test with injected 429s and 500s
Explain idempotency for tool side-effects
modules.deliverable: A hardened client with a chaos-test suite.

modules.title: Cost, Latency, Privacy & Model Selection
modules.why: Choosing models is an engineering economics problem: quality per dollar per millisecond, plus data policy.
objectives: Estimate and measure cost per request
completion: Produce a cost/latency table for one workload across 3 models
Justify a routing rule in writing
modules.deliverable: Model-selection decision record for your project.

modules.title: Checkpoint Project: Tool-Using Assistant
modules.why: Portfolio proof of LLM engineering: validated outputs, real tools, measured cost and latency.
completion: Runs from a stranger's terminal with only a README
modules.deliverable: Portfolio project #3 (see Projects page).

modules.title: Document Ingestion & Parsing
modules.why: RAG quality is capped by what you manage to extract from source documents — tables, PDFs, and layout included.
completion: Ingest a 100-doc mixed corpus with zero silent failures
modules.deliverable: An ingestion pipeline with per-document status reports.

modules.title: Chunking Strategies & Metadata
modules.why: Chunk boundaries decide retrieval granularity; done badly, perfect embeddings still return garbage.
completion: A/B two chunking strategies with hit-rate@5 on 20 queries
modules.deliverable: Chunking experiment write-up with numbers.

modules.title: Embedding Models & Vector Databases
modules.why: The storage and lookup layer of semantic memory — in agents, in RAG, in recommendations.
completion: Explain HNSW trade-offs in two sentences
Serve semantic search under 50 ms on 100k chunks
modules.deliverable: A queryable vector index over your corpus.

modules.title: Hybrid Retrieval, Query Transforms & Reranking
modules.why: Production retrieval combines keyword precision with semantic recall, then reranks — this is where quality jumps.
completion: Beat your dense-only baseline on hit-rate@5 with hybrid+rerank
modules.deliverable: Retrieval upgrade experiment with eval table.

modules.title: Citations, Grounding & Hallucination Reduction
modules.why: Users trust what they can verify; citations and grounding turn a text generator into a knowledge system.
completion: Every answer sentence traceable to a source or refused
modules.deliverable: Grounding checks integrated into your pipeline.

modules.title: RAG Evaluation & Observability
modules.why: You cannot improve what you don't measure; eval harnesses are the resume-differentiator of AI engineering.
completion: A 30-question eval suite wired into CI
modules.deliverable: Eval harness + dashboard for your RAG app.

modules.title: Checkpoint Project: Document Q&A with Citations
modules.why: The flagship RAG portfolio piece: cited answers over your own documents with published quality numbers.
objectives: Full pipeline: ingest → retrieve → answer → cite
completion: Demo survives a stranger asking adversarial questions
modules.deliverable: Portfolio project #4 (see Projects page).

modules.title: Chatbots vs Workflows vs Agents
modules.why: Naming the architecture you need is the first engineering decision of every AI project.
objectives: Define agent vs workflow vs chatbot precisely
completion: Classify 10 real products correctly and justify each
modules.deliverable: An architecture-decision note for your own project.

modules.title: The Agent Loop: Observe–Reason–Act–Evaluate
modules.why: Every agent framework is this loop wearing a costume; owning it bare-metal makes frameworks transparent.
objectives: Implement the loop from scratch (no framework)
completion: Framework-free agent completes a 3-tool task
Explain each loop field's role from memory
modules.deliverable: A ~100-line agent loop you fully understand.

modules.title: Tool Selection, Design & Execution Safety
modules.why: Tools are your agent's hands; bad tool design causes most real-world agent failures.
objectives: Design tool APIs models use correctly
Schemas, defaults, and error messages for models
completion: Redesign one bad tool and measure selection accuracy gains
modules.deliverable: A tool-design checklist applied to your own tools.

modules.title: Planning, Decomposition & State
modules.why: Multi-step competence requires explicit plans and durable state — the difference between demos and reliability.
objectives: Explicit state machines vs free-form loops
completion: Convert a flaky free-form agent into a stateful, resumable one
modules.deliverable: A state-diagram (Mermaid) plus checkpointed implementation.

modules.title: Short-Term & Long-Term Memory
modules.why: Context is scarce and expensive; memory systems are how agents stay coherent across sessions without gold-plating every prompt.
completion: Agent maintains coherence across a 50-turn session within budget
modules.deliverable: A memory layer with compaction you can demonstrate.

modules.title: Reflection & Controlled Retries
modules.why: Self-correction with limits: reflection improves quality, unbounded reflection melts your budget.
objectives: Retry with error feedback (not blind retries)
completion: A/B reflection on a 20-task suite; keep only if it pays
modules.deliverable: Reflection experiment with cost/quality data.

modules.title: Deterministic Workflows & Human-in-the-Loop
modules.why: Real deployments put humans before irreversible actions and rails around the rest.
completion: Design an approval flow for a sensitive action with rollback
modules.deliverable: A HITL design doc for your capstone.

modules.title: LangChain & LangGraph Orchestration
modules.why: Your primary framework: LangGraph models agents as state graphs — exactly the mental model you built bare-metal.
completion: Rebuild your bare-metal agent in LangGraph with an interrupt
modules.deliverable: A LangGraph agent repo with graph diagram in README.

modules.title: MCP Servers & Clients
modules.why: MCP is becoming the USB-C of AI tooling — write tools once, plug into any client.
objectives: Build and expose an MCP server
Consume MCP tools from your agent
completion: Your capstone exposes one tool via MCP and consumes one external server
modules.deliverable: A documented MCP server for your domain.

modules.title: Multi-Agent Architectures
modules.why: Optional specialisation: powerful for scale, seductive to over-use. Learn when a single agent with good tools wins.
completion: Justify (or reject) multi-agent design in a written trade-off note
modules.deliverable: A multi-agent demo plus a single-agent counterfactual.

modules.title: Checkpoint Projects: The Agent Suite
modules.why: Four smaller agent projects that jointly prove planning, retrieval, analysis, and human-approval skills.
objectives: Data analyst agent on real datasets
Workflow with approval before sensitive actions
completion: Each has an eval set and a recorded demo
modules.deliverable: Agent suite feeding your capstone and portfolio.

modules.title: FastAPI & Backend Architecture
modules.why: Your React skills meet Python: FastAPI is how agents become services with typed contracts.
completion: Serve your Phase-4 assistant over a typed streaming API
modules.deliverable: A FastAPI service with OpenAPI docs and tests.

modules.title: Auth, Databases & Conversation State
modules.why: Multi-user agents need identities, sessions, and durable conversation history.
objectives: JWT/OAuth flows at a working level
completion: Two users with isolated histories on your deployed service
modules.deliverable: Auth + persistence layer with migration scripts.

modules.title: Docker & Environment Configuration
modules.why: Docker is the unit of deployment everywhere; reproducible envs end "works on my machine".
objectives: Dockerfile best practices for Python AI apps
Config via env vars, never baked secrets
completion: One-command local start of your full stack via compose
modules.deliverable: Published images + compose file.

modules.title: Cloud Deployment
modules.why: A public URL transforms a repo into a portfolio artefact recruiters can actually try.
objectives: Deploy the container (Railway/Render/Fly or a VM)
completion: Live public demo with uptime monitoring
modules.deliverable: Your service, deployed and linked from your README.

modules.title: Logging, Tracing & Monitoring
modules.why: You cannot debug what you cannot see; traces are how agent failures become diagnosable.
completion: Trace one failing agent run end-to-end from a dashboard
modules.deliverable: An observability stack on your capstone.

modules.title: Tests, Integration & Agent Evaluations
modules.why: Agent behaviour needs regression suites exactly like code does — this is rare and hireable skill.
objectives: Eval suites in CI with golden datasets
completion: CI fails when agent quality regresses beyond threshold
modules.deliverable: A CI-integrated eval pipeline.

modules.title: Security: Injection, Tools & Data Leakage
modules.why: Prompt injection is the SQL injection of this decade; safe tool design is the defence.
completion: Break your own agent with an injection, then fix it
modules.deliverable: A security review document with red-team transcript.

modules.title: Budgets, Fallbacks & Reliability
modules.why: Production agents must fail gracefully and cost predictably under real traffic.
objectives: Cost budgets and caps per session/task
completion: Survive a load test within budget with graceful degradation
modules.deliverable: Reliability report with load-test graphs.

modules.title: CI/CD & Maintenance
modules.why: Optional depth: automated pipelines keep quality high while you keep learning.
completion: Ship a change via PR with tests, evals, and preview
modules.deliverable: A working pipeline file in your capstone repo.

modules.title: Capstone: Secure Deployed Agent
modules.why: The interview centrepiece: an agent that is deployed, evaluated, monitored, and hardened.
objectives: Combine Phase 6 agent suite + Phase 7 infrastructure
completion: A stranger can use it; an engineer can trace it; you can defend every choice
modules.deliverable: Portfolio project #5 (see Projects page).

modules.title: Portfolio Assembly (3–5 Projects)
modules.why: Depth beats quantity: a few projects with real engineering stories outweigh a wall of tutorials.
objectives: Select and polish the strongest 3–5 projects
completion: Each project has demo, diagram, numbers, and clean README
modules.deliverable: A portfolio section on your GitHub profile site.

modules.title: READMEs, Demos & Technical Storytelling
modules.why: Recruiters spend 90 seconds per repo; writing and demo craft decide what they see.
completion: A stranger understands each project in 2 minutes
modules.deliverable: Three polished READMEs + one recorded demo.

modules.title: Interview Preparation
modules.why: Convert projects into offers: system design, agent debugging scenarios, and honest depth signals.
completion: Pass a mock interview for each target role
modules.deliverable: An interview story bank per project.

modules.title: Final Review & Job-Readiness Assessment
modules.why: Close the loop: measure readiness against the role bar and set the next learning horizon.
objectives: Gap plan for the first 90 days on the job
completion: Written readiness verdict with evidence
modules.deliverable: Your job-readiness report — the final artefact.

modules.title: How a model reads your prompt
modules.why: Every prompt failure you will debug — vagueness, drift, hallucination — is easier to fix once you stop thinking of the model as a person and start thinking of it as a next-token predictor reading everything you gave it, literally.
objectives: Explain tokens, the context window, and why wording changes outcomes
Describe what "the model has no memory of you" means for prompt design
Predict which of two phrasings is more likely to steer a model
completion: Can explain next-token prediction without hand-waving
Ran the same instruction with 3 wordings and logged the differences
Wrote a one-paragraph mental model in your own words
modules.deliverable: A short note: "what the model actually sees when I send my prompt".

modules.title: Anatomy of a prompt
modules.why: Most bad prompts are good ingredients in the wrong order. The instruction / context / input / output-format skeleton turns prompt writing from art into assembly.
objectives: Decompose any prompt into its four anatomical parts
Reorder a messy prompt into the skeleton and compare results
Write an output-format spec the first time, not after the third retry
completion: Rewrote 5 of your own prompts into the skeleton
Produced a before/after diff with output examples
Can identify the missing part in a broken prompt on sight
modules.deliverable: Annotated before/after of five real prompts.

modules.title: System, developer & user roles
modules.why: Role messages are the priority system of prompting: they decide what wins when instructions conflict. Misunderstanding them is the root cause of "the model ignores my instructions".
objectives: Explain the precedence of system, developer, and user messages
Move task rules into the system role without losing specificity
Recognise role-conflict failures in real transcripts
completion: Rebuilt a chat prompt with rules correctly split across roles
Documented one conflict case and how you resolved it
modules.deliverable: A role-layout template you will reuse in every later project.

modules.title: Clarity, specificity & constraints
modules.why: "Make it better" is not a task. Verbs, constraints, audience, and length bounds are the dials that make model output reproducible — and testable in Phase 4.
objectives: Replace vague adjectives with measurable constraints
State audience, tone, format, and length explicitly
Turn a one-line request into a specification
completion: Converted 10 vague requests into specifications
A/B-tested one constraint change and recorded the effect
modules.deliverable: A constraint checklist card next to your keyboard.

modules.title: Delimiters & structure
modules.why: Delimiters tell the model where data ends and instructions begin — the first line of defense against confused output and, later, against injection.
objectives: Choose and apply consistent delimiters for data blocks
Explain how delimiters reduce instruction/data confusion
completion: Reformatted one prompt to clearly separate data from instructions
Wrote your delimiter convention down and used it twice
modules.deliverable: Your written delimiter convention, used in the next 3 modules.

modules.title: Zero-shot task patterns
modules.why: Classify, extract, rewrite, translate, summarise, generate — most production prompts are instances of a handful of task shapes. Recognising the shape gives you a proven starting point.
objectives: Name the task shape behind any request
Apply the matching zero-shot pattern for each shape
Know which shapes need structure (Phase 2) or examples (Phase 3)
completion: Built a personal cheat-sheet of 6 task patterns
Shipped 3 prompts from the sheet against real inputs
modules.deliverable: A one-page pattern cheat-sheet with one worked example each.

modules.title: Chat UIs vs the API surface
modules.why: Chat interfaces hide the knobs that matter: temperature, max tokens, stop sequences, system access. Engineering prompts means living on the API side of the fence.
objectives: Send your first API request with a system prompt and parameters
Explain what temperature does and does not control
Reproduce a chat-UI result in an API call
completion: Ran the same prompt at temperature 0 and 1 and diffed outputs
Can read an API request body line by line
modules.deliverable: A tiny script that calls a model with your skeleton prompt.

modules.title: Why structured output beats prose
modules.why: The moment a program consumes model output, free text becomes a liability. This module frames prompts as APIs: consumers, contracts, and failure modes.
objectives: Argue the contract view of prompting with examples
Identify downstream consumers of an output
List the failure modes of prose output for programs
completion: Mapped one real task from prose to structured output
Documented the consumer and its contract
modules.deliverable: A before/after case study: prose answer vs parsed object.

modules.title: JSON mode & guaranteed syntax
modules.why: Hoping for valid JSON and getting valid JSON are different engineering positions. You learn what JSON modes actually guarantee — and what they leave to you.
objectives: Enable and test JSON mode on a real API call
Explain syntax guarantee vs schema guarantee
Handle the "guaranteed JSON, wrong shape" trap
completion: 50/50 calls returned parseable JSON in your harness
Wrote up what JSON mode did and did not fix
modules.deliverable: A minimal JSON-mode request with a parse step.

modules.title: Designing schemas the model can satisfy
modules.why: Models fail schemas that are ambiguous, over-nested, or human-unfriendly. Schema design is prompt design: field names are instructions.
objectives: Design flat, unambiguous schemas with pydantic or zod
Choose enums over free text wherever possible
Name fields so the model needs no extra explanation
completion: Authored 3 schemas for real tasks
Improved one schema until failure rate dropped measurably
modules.deliverable: Three versioned schemas with comments on design choices.

modules.title: Function & tool calling as prompting
modules.why: Tool definitions are prompts in structured clothing. Understanding tool schemas makes you better at both structured output and, later, agent prompting.
objectives: Define a tool the model calls correctly on the first try
Describe the role of tool names, descriptions, and parameter schemas
Handle the no-match and multi-match cases explicitly
completion: A working tool-call round trip with argument validation
Documented one description rewrite that fixed wrong calls
modules.deliverable: One tool with a before/after description experiment.

modules.title: Validate-and-repair loops
modules.why: Production pipelines do not trust the model; they check its work and send failures back with the errors attached. The repair loop is the pattern that turns 92% into 99%.
objectives: Validate output against a schema programmatically
Feed validation errors back into a repair prompt
Bound retries and decide when to fail loudly
completion: Implemented a repair loop over 50 real inputs
Reported first-pass vs post-repair success rates
modules.deliverable: A repair-loop function with measured before/after rates.

modules.title: Extraction pipelines
modules.why: Extraction is the most-shipped LLM feature in industry. It combines everything so far: schema, validation, repair, and honest measurement.
objectives: Build an end-to-end extractor for a messy real corpus
Handle empty, multi-item, and adversarial inputs
completion: Labeled 20 gold items and scored your extractor
Fixed the top error class and re-scored
modules.deliverable: An extraction pipeline with a scorecard — the Phase-2 checkpoint.

modules.title: Streaming & partial parsing
modules.why: Latency is a feature. Streaming structured output without breaking the UX is a real production skill — and simpler than it sounds once you know the tricks.
objectives: Stream tokens to a UI while assembling the object
Parse incrementally or show progress honestly
Explain the trade-offs of streaming vs batch for structured tasks
completion: A streamed response rendered progressively in a tiny UI
One paragraph on when you would NOT stream
modules.deliverable: A streaming demo with graceful loading states.

modules.title: The context budget
modules.why: Tokens are money and attention. Deciding what deserves space — and what gets summarised or dropped — is the core economic skill of prompting.
objectives: Audit a real prompt and cut it without losing quality
Measure quality before and after a budget cut
completion: Cut one prompt by 40% with no measurable quality loss
Documented your priority order for a real product
modules.deliverable: A budget audit on your own worst prompt.

modules.title: Few-shot examples that teach
modules.why: Examples are the highest-leverage tokens in most prompts — and badly chosen ones actively mislead. Selection, count, ordering, and edge coverage is a system, not a vibe.
objectives: Choose examples that cover the decision boundary
Decide how many examples to include and when to stop
completion: Ran a 0/1/3/5-shot comparison on one task
Replaced a long instruction with two good examples
modules.deliverable: A few-shot experiment table: shots vs accuracy vs tokens.

modules.title: Reasoning patterns: CoT & friends
modules.why: Asking for steps changes accuracy on hard tasks. You learn chain-of-thought, least-to-most, and self-consistency — and when each helps or wastes tokens.
objectives: Apply CoT to a task and measure the delta
Split a hard task into least-to-most sub-prompts
Know when reasoning prompts make output worse
completion: Measured CoT vs direct on 20 items
Documented a case where CoT hurt
modules.deliverable: A reasoning-pattern decision table with your own numbers.

modules.title: Personas & priming — and their limits
modules.why: "You are a senior tax lawyer" is everywhere, and mostly cargo cult. You learn what personas actually move, what they do not, and how to test the difference.
objectives: Test persona effects on style vs accuracy separately
Replace persona claims with capability instructions
Spot the sycophancy failure mode priming can cause
completion: A/B-tested persona vs no-persona on 20 items
Rewrote one persona into concrete instructions
modules.deliverable: A persona test write-up with an honest verdict.

modules.title: Long-context strategy
modules.why: Big context windows did not end context engineering — position matters (lost-in-the-middle), and dumping everything is slow and expensive. Structure beats size.
objectives: Explain positional bias with a reproduction
Chunk and outline documents instead of pasting them
Decide between stuffing, map-reduce, and retrieval
completion: Reproduced lost-in-the-middle on a real model
Restructured one long-context task with better results
modules.deliverable: A long-context strategy note with your reproduction numbers.

modules.title: Grounding: RAG prompt patterns
modules.why: Retrieval decides what the model sees; the prompt decides what it does with it. Grounding instructions, citation formats, and honest refusals are what make RAG trustworthy.
objectives: Require inline citations in a parseable format
Design the "not in the sources" refusal path
completion: A grounded prompt with citations on 20 questions
Refusal rate measured on out-of-scope questions
modules.deliverable: A grounded Q&A prompt + refusal test results.

modules.title: Conversation memory & summarisation
modules.why: Multi-turn products leak context, forget constraints, and balloon costs. Rolling summaries, restated constraints, and selective history are how you stay coherent and cheap.
objectives: Keep constraints alive across turns explicitly
Bound history size without losing the plot
completion: A 10-turn conversation that kept its constraints
A summariser prompt with a quality check
modules.deliverable: A memory scheme diagram plus its summariser prompt.

modules.title: Vibe-checking is not testing
modules.why: Without a golden set, every prompt change is a coin flip dressed as progress. This module installs the test-first habit that makes everything after it science.
objectives: Build a golden set of 20-50 real items with expected outputs
Run your first scored comparison of two prompts
completion: Golden set stored as data, not vibes
Two prompts scored head-to-head on it
modules.deliverable: A golden set file + your first scoreboard.

modules.title: Metrics: exact, judge & human
modules.why: Exact match, programmatic checks, LLM-as-judge, and human review each fit different tasks. Choosing the wrong metric wastes weeks; calibrating a judge is a skill.
objectives: Pick the cheapest metric that reflects the task
Build and calibrate an LLM-as-judge against your own labels
Know when only a human counts
completion: Judge agrees with your labels at a measured rate
Documented metric choice per task type
modules.deliverable: A calibrated judge prompt with agreement stats.

modules.title: Regression suites & prompt versioning
modules.why: Prompts are code. Version them, diff them, and never ship an edit that silently breaks a case you already fixed.
objectives: Store prompts as versioned files with changelogs
Run the eval suite on every change automatically
Bisect a regression to the exact prompt edit
completion: A repo where prompt edits trigger evals
Found and fixed one regression you introduced on purpose
modules.deliverable: A versioned prompt repo with an eval script.

modules.title: Error analysis & taxonomy
modules.why: A 78% score is a rumor; a table of error classes is a plan. You learn to bucket failures and match each bucket to its fix — prompt, schema, examples, or model.
objectives: Label every golden-set failure with a category
Map each category to its fix layer
Decide when the model, not the prompt, is the problem
completion: An error taxonomy for one real project
Top error class fixed and re-scored
modules.deliverable: An error-analysis report with before/after scores.

modules.title: Systematic prompt optimization
modules.why: Beyond manual iteration: A/B grids, self-refinement, generated instruction search. You learn the methods that scale when you have 20 prompts, not one.
objectives: Run a structured A/B grid over prompt variants
Use self-critique to refine a prompt automatically
Know when optimization overfits the golden set
completion: A grid search over at least 6 variants, scored
One overfitting case caught with a held-out split
modules.deliverable: An optimization run log with a train/held-out split.

modules.title: Cost & latency engineering
modules.why: The best prompt is often the cheapest one that passes evals. Caching, model routing, token budgets, and batch modes turn a demo into a bill you can afford.
objectives: Compute cost per 1k requests for a real prompt
Apply caching and routing to cut spend measurably
Trade latency vs quality explicitly with numbers
completion: A cost model spreadsheet for one product
A routing change with quality held constant
modules.deliverable: A cost/latency report for one real pipeline.

modules.title: Prompts in CI
modules.why: The endgame: prompt changes gated by evals in continuous integration, so a regression is a red build — not a support ticket three days later.
objectives: Wire an eval run into CI on prompt-file changes
Gate merges on a minimum score threshold
completion: A PR that fails CI due to a prompt regression
Thresholds documented per suite

modules.title: Prompt injection: direct & indirect
modules.why: Anything that puts text into your prompt — a webpage, an email, a PDF — is an attacker writing part of your prompt. Injection is the vulnerability class of the LLM era.
objectives: Execute a direct injection against your own demo
Plant an indirect injection in retrieved content
Explain why "just say no to instructions" prompts fail
completion: Two working attacks documented step by step
A clear explanation of why instruction-listing defenses leak
modules.deliverable: A personal injection-lab repo with reproducible attacks.

modules.title: System-prompt leakage & exfiltration
modules.why: Your system prompt is your product logic — and sometimes your secrets. Leakage and data-exfiltration channels turn prompt theft into real breaches.
objectives: Extract a hidden system prompt with classic tricks
Identify exfiltration channels in a chat product
Decide what genuinely must never live in a prompt
completion: One successful extraction, written up
A policy note: what belongs in prompts vs server code
modules.deliverable: A leakage post-mortem on your own demo.

modules.title: Defense in depth
modules.why: No single prompt fix stops injection. Layered defenses — privilege separation, allow-lists, approval gates, sandboxing — assume the prompt falls and contain the blast radius.
objectives: Design a privilege-separated architecture for an assistant
Apply allow-lists and approval gates to tool actions
Explain what each layer does and does not stop
completion: A defense diagram with layers labeled
Your earlier attacks re-run against layered defenses
modules.deliverable: A layered-defense design doc with attack/defense matrix.

modules.title: Spotlighting & data/instruction separation
modules.why: Marking untrusted data so the model can tell it apart from instructions is a practical, measurable defense family: delimiters, datamarking, and encoding.
objectives: Apply delimiters + explicit contracts to untrusted text
Try datamarking/encoding variants and measure break rates
completion: Break-rate table for 3 spotlighting variants
Chosen variant documented with its limits
modules.deliverable: A spotlighting comparison with measured break rates.

modules.title: Red-teaming your own prompts
modules.why: Attack yourself on a schedule, with a method — before users, scrapers, or competitors do it for you.
objectives: Run a structured red-team session: roles, vectors, time-boxes
Log findings with severity and reproduction
Convert findings into eval cases and defenses
completion: 10+ findings logged and triaged
Top 3 converted into regression evals
modules.deliverable: A red-team report — the Phase-5 checkpoint artifact.

modules.title: Guardrails & output filtering
modules.why: Filters and classifiers catch what prompts miss — and create false positives and latency of their own. Guardrails are a layer, not a religion.
objectives: Add an output filter to one pipeline
Decide fail-open vs fail-closed per use case
completion: A filter with measured error rates
A written fail-open/fail-closed policy
modules.deliverable: A guardrail implementation + error-rate table.

modules.title: Responsible prompting: PII, bias, disclosure
modules.why: Prompts touch personal data, encode bias, and shape decisions about people. The professional prompt engineer knows the obligations, not just the tricks.
objectives: Redact and minimise PII flowing through prompts
Test outputs for biased patterns across groups
Apply disclosure rules for AI-generated content
completion: A PII handling checklist applied to one project
A bias probe run with results recorded
modules.deliverable: A responsible-use checklist wired into your workflow.

modules.title: Playbook: search & answering
modules.why: Question answering over documents is the highest-volume LLM product. The playbook: query understanding, grounding, citations, refusals, and follow-ups.
objectives: Assemble the full QA prompt stack from earlier modules
Score the stack on a 30-question benchmark
completion: 30-question benchmark with a scorecard
Clarifying-question behavior demonstrated

modules.title: Playbook: summarisation at scale
modules.why: Summarisation sounds trivial; at scale it is chunking, budgets, faithfulness checks, and format control per audience.
objectives: Pick map-reduce vs refine for a real corpus
Check faithfulness with a judge or checklist
completion: 100-document corpus summarised with consistent format
Faithfulness spot-check results recorded
modules.deliverable: A summarisation playbook with a faithfulness check.

modules.title: Playbook: code generation & review
modules.why: Code prompts reward structure more than any other domain: context layout, diff formats, test-first framing, and review prompts that catch real bugs.
objectives: Design a code-gen prompt with tests as the spec
Write a review prompt with a bug taxonomy
Measure pass-rate on a small task set
completion: 10-task pass-rate measured for your prompt
One review-prompt bug catch demonstrated

modules.title: Playbook: prompting agents & tools
modules.why: Agents are prompts with consequences. System prompts for tool loops, plan formats, stop conditions, and the approval gates from Phase 5 — the bridge to the AI Agents roadmap.
objectives: Write a system prompt that drives a tool loop reliably
Define plan-then-act behavior and stop conditions
Add an approval gate for destructive tools
completion: An agent loop that survives 3 messy real tasks
Approval gate demonstrated on one destructive tool

modules.title: Playbook: content, brand & tone
modules.why: Marketing content at scale needs brand voice as a schema, not a vibe — plus variation control and legal-safe generation.
objectives: Encode a brand voice as explicit instructions + examples
Generate controlled variations with measurable tone shifts

completion: A voice spec a stranger can apply consistently
Variation set judged on-tone at a measured rate

modules.title: Playbook: text-to-SQL & data analysis
modules.why: Natural language to queries is high-value and high-risk: schemas in context, validation of generated SQL, and read-only guardrails.
objectives: Present a database schema compactly in context
Enforce read-only access and measure success rate
completion: 20-question query benchmark with pass rate
One rejected dangerous query demonstrated

modules.title: Capstone: your eval-backed prompt library
modules.why: The portfolio artifact: a public, versioned library of playbook prompts, each with evals, changelogs, and honest limitations — proof you engineer prompts, not type them.
objectives: Publish 8+ patterns with evals and docs
Include the red-team report and cost notes
Write the README that makes engineers trust it
completion: Library public with passing CI on evals
README follows the portfolio skeleton

modules.deliverable: The public prompt library — your interview centerpiece.

lessons.title: The Agent Loop
lessons.tagline: Every agent framework is this one loop wearing a costume.
simple: An AI agent is a program that repeatedly asks a large language model "what should I do next?" and actually does it. That is almost the whole idea. The model cannot run code, search the web, or send emails by itself — it can only write text. So your program gives the model a list of tools it may ask for, plus the current situation, and the model replies with either a final answer or a request to call one of the tools.

Your code executes that tool, attaches the result back into the conversation, and asks the model again. Round and round it goes — until the model produces a final answer, or a limit you set is reached. The loop is the agent. Frameworks like LangGraph wrap this loop with nicer state management, but underneath, this is all they do.

intuition.analogy: A brilliant intern with a phone, working for you remotely.
paragraphs: The intern (the model) is extremely well-read and reasons well, but has no hands: they cannot open your files, browse, or send messages themselves. You give them a goal ("find out why churn spiked and brief me"), a phone directory of people who can do things (the tools), and a rule: check in before doing anything irreversible.

The intern calls you with requests ("phone the analytics desk"), you place the call and read them the answer (tool execution → observation), and they continue reasoning. Eventually they hand you the brief (final answer). If they ramble for hours, you cut them off (max steps). If they want to publish something to customers, you approve it first (human-in-the-loop).

technical: Formally, an agent is a state machine over a message history M and a tool set T = {t₁…tₙ}, each tool described by a JSON schema. Each iteration: send M + tool schemas to the model; the model returns either a tool call (name + arguments) or a final completion. The orchestrator validates arguments, executes the tool, appends the result as a tool-role message (the observation), and loops.

The stopping conditions are engineering decisions, not model decisions: a final answer, a maximum step count, a token/cost budget, or an interrupt (approval gate). Observations are just messages — which means context grows every step, attention cost grows quadratically, and older steps can be summarised or dropped (compaction).

Note what the model never does: it never executes anything. It emits structured requests; your runtime holds the privileges. This separation — decisions in the model, execution in your code — is the security boundary you will defend in Phase 7.
deeper: Context growth is the loop's hidden quadratic tax. Each step re-sends the whole history, and transformer attention over n tokens costs O(n²) time and O(n) memory per layer — so step 40 of a long agent run is dramatically more expensive per token than step 1, before you even count the extra input tokens themselves. This is why serious agent runtimes compact: summarise older tool results, keep structured digests of observations, or move long outputs to external scratch files referenced by path.

ReAct vs plan-and-execute are the two canonical loop shapes. ReAct (Reason+Act) interleaves thinking and tool calls step by step — flexible, but prone to drift on long tasks. Plan-and-execute produces an explicit plan first, then executes items (sometimes re-planning after each) — more deterministic and easier to resume, at the cost of adaptability. Most production systems are hybrids: a plan skeleton with local ReAct-style flexibility inside each step.

Formally, the loop defines a Markov decision process where the policy is the model conditioned on the message history, actions are tool calls ∪ {final}, and the reward is implicit in your stopping rules and evaluation harness. You don't train this policy — you engineer around it: tool design shapes the action space, prompts shape the policy, and budgets shape the horizon.
realWorld: Claude Code and similar coding agents are this loop with tools like "read file", "edit file", and "run command" — plus approval gates exactly like the one in the Playground.
Customer-support agents loop over tools like look_up_order, check_refund_policy, and issue_refund; the irreversible tool always sits behind a rule or a human.
LangGraph's graph runtime, OpenAI's agent loops, and MCP clients all reduce to this structure — which is why you build it once, framework-free, before touching any framework.

lessons.title: Embeddings & Similarity
lessons.tagline: Turn meaning into geometry — the most reused idea in applied AI.
simple: An embedding is a list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of a piece of text. The trick: texts with similar meanings get vectors that point in similar directions. "Cats chase laser pointers" and "Felines pursue blinking lights" are different words, but their vectors end up close together — while "Interest rates rose this quarter" points somewhere entirely different.

Nobody types these numbers by hand. An embedding model (a small neural network) is trained on huge amounts of text so that it produces this geometry. Once you have vectors, "how similar are these two texts?" becomes arithmetic you already know: multiply and add.

intuition.analogy: A library where shelves are arranged by meaning, not alphabet.
paragraphs: Every book gets a position on a giant map: cooking books cluster in one region, astrophysics in another, and a book about "the chemistry of cooking" sits between them. To find books similar to yours, you do not read every book — you look at what is nearby on the map.

A vector is just coordinates on that map (with hundreds of dimensions instead of two). Cosine similarity answers "how close to the same shelf?" — and search, RAG retrieval, deduplication, and agent memory are all, at heart, "find me the neighbours".

technical: An embedding model f: text → ℝᵈ maps sequences to d-dimensional vectors (384–3,072 dims are typical). Training objectives (contrastive losses, masked-language objectives) shape the space so semantically related inputs land near each other; normalising vectors to unit length makes dot product equal cosine similarity.

Cosine similarity cos(a, b) = a·b / (|a||b|) measures the angle between vectors: 1 = same direction, 0 = unrelated (orthogonal), −1 = opposite. Cosine ignores magnitude — useful because a long document is not "more about its topic" than a short one; length is not meaning.

Search over millions of vectors uses approximate nearest neighbour indexes (HNSW and friends) that trade a little recall for orders-of-magnitude speed-up — the machinery behind every vector database you will meet in Phase 5.
deeper: Embedding models are trained with contrastive objectives: pull annotated paraphrase pairs together, push random (negative) pairs apart — InfoNCE loss is the common formulation. The quality of a retrieval system is largely decided by how well the embedding model's training distribution matches your documents; a model trained on web paragraphs may underperform on legal text or code without domain-tuned alternatives.

HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) indexes build layered proximity graphs: upper layers are sparse "highways" for long jumps, lower layers dense for precision. Search descends greedily layer by layer — O(log n) hops in practice, at the cost of memory-heavy graphs and no exact guarantees. That is the concrete meaning of "approximate" nearest neighbour, and why vector DBs expose an ef_search dial trading recall for latency.

Why cosine rather than dot product or Euclidean? With unit-normalised vectors, all three give identical rankings — the choice is really about raw vectors, where magnitude encodes length/token-count signal you usually do not want ranking your results. The professional habit: normalise once at ingest, then think purely in angles.
lessons.walkthroughCode:
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import numpy as np

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")

docs = ["Cats chase laser pointers.",
        "Felines pursue blinking lights.",
        "Interest rates rose this quarter."]

V = model.encode(docs, normalize_embeddings=True)

sim = V @ V.T
print(np.round(sim, 2))
realWorld: Your Netflix recommendation project used collaborative filtering ("users like you liked…"); embeddings add content-based similarity ("items like this…"). Modern recommenders blend both.
Every RAG system (Phase 5) is this lesson at scale: embed chunks once, embed the query, take the top-k neighbours, and hand them to the LLM as context.
Agent memory (Phase 6) uses the same trick: past conversations are embedded and retrieved when relevant, instead of stuffing everything into the context window.

lessons.title: What the Model Actually Sees
lessons.tagline: A prompt is not a message to a person — it is the entire world, for exactly one call.
simple: When you send a prompt, the model does not remember you, your previous chats, or your intentions. Everything it knows this turn is the exact text you sent — nothing more.

That text is first chopped into tokens: word pieces of roughly four characters each. "Unbelievable" might be three tokens; "the" is one. The model never sees letters or spacing the way you do — only this token sequence.
The model then does one job: predict the next token, again and again, until it decides to stop. Every word it writes is chosen from probabilities computed over everything you gave it.
This is why two wordings of the "same" request produce different answers. They are different token sequences, so the probabilities differ — even at temperature 0.

And it is why structure beats politeness. A clear instruction, well-separated data, and an explicit output format change the probabilities far more reliably than "please" or "you are the world's best expert".

intuition.analogy: The model is a brilliant consultant with amnesia who reads exactly one brief.
paragraphs: Imagine hiring a genius consultant who, each morning, has forgotten every previous meeting. You communicate only by sliding a single sheet of paper under their door, and they slide back one answer. That sheet is your prompt.

A vague sheet — "make our product sound good" — gets a generic answer, because the consultant must guess everything you left unsaid. A precise sheet — audience, length, tone, format, the source material, clearly marked — gets the answer you actually wanted, because all of it is on the one page they will ever see.

The sheet also has a size limit (the context window). If you stuff it with irrelevant pages, the important lines do not get "read more carefully" — they compete with noise. Budgeting that page is a core skill of this roadmap.

technical: A prompt enters a chat-shaped API as a list of messages with roles (system, developer, user, assistant). Higher-priority roles win when instructions conflict, which is why persistent rules belong in the system message, not re-sent per turn.

The tokenizer maps your text to token ids. Tokenization explains several quirks: why models are bad at counting letters in a word, why "strawberry" puzzles them, and why a small wording change can shift output — it changes the token boundary structure.
The context window is a hard budget counted in tokens. Model output also draws from it, so a 4,000-token answer in an 8,000-token window halves the room your input has.

Attention is computed across the whole window, but not uniformly: position matters. Content buried in the middle of very long prompts is retrieved less reliably than content at the start or end — the "lost in the middle" effect you will reproduce in Phase 3.

Temperature controls the randomness of sampling over the predicted distribution; it does not change what the model knows. At temperature 0 the same token sequence still yields the same output — which is why your test harnesses fix it.
deeper: At each step the model outputs a probability distribution over the vocabulary (often 50k-200k tokens) via a softmax over logits. Sampling at temperature T divides logit differences by T before the softmax: lower T sharpens the distribution, higher T flattens it.
This is why temperature 0 is deterministic but not "correct" — it is greedy argmax over the same distribution. If the prompt is ambiguous, the most probable continuation may still be a guess.
Some APIs expose the top logprobs per generated token. Reading them is the cheapest way to see whether the model was confident or coin-flipping — a tool you will use for eval diagnostics in Phase 4.
lessons.walkthroughCode:
import OpenAI from 'openai'
const client = new OpenAI() // key stays server-side in real apps

const VAGUE = 'Write about our product.'
const SPECIFIED = [
  'Write a 2-sentence product description.',
  'Audience: backend engineers. Tone: technical, no hype.',
  'Include exactly one concrete feature. Present tense.',
  'Output format: plain prose, no heading, no emoji.',
].join('\n')

for (const temperature of [0, 1]) {
  const res = await client.chat.completions.create({
    model: 'gpt-4o-mini',
    temperature,
    messages: [{ role: 'user', content: VAGUE }],
  })
  console.log(temperature, '->', res.choices[0].message.content)
}
realWorld: Support-ticket triage: the same classifier prompt runs thousands of times a day; understanding variance is what makes its output trustworthy enough to route on.
Data extraction pipelines: every field must come from the input document alone — the mental model of "the prompt is the whole world" is literally the security boundary.
Interviews: "why did the model ignore my instruction?" is answered by role precedence and token-level input understanding — a favourite screening question.

lessons.title: JSON You Can Trust
lessons.tagline: JSON mode guarantees syntax. Your program needs a schema, a validator, and a repair loop.
simple: The moment a program consumes model output, free text becomes a liability. The program needs an object with known fields, known types, and known allowed values — a schema.

JSON mode (or structured-output modes) guarantees the response parses as JSON. That sounds like enough. It is not: a response can be valid JSON and still have a missing field, a string where you expected a number, or an invented value outside your enum.

Syntax guarantee and shape guarantee are different promises. You close the gap yourself: validate every response against a schema in code (pydantic or zod), and when validation fails, send the errors back to the model with a repair instruction.

The repair loop is the pattern that turns 92% first-pass reliability into 99%+: validate, show the model exactly which constraint it violated, validate again. Usually one round is enough; always bound the retries.
Design the schema to be easy to satisfy: flat beats nested, enums beat free text, and field names that say what they mean ("country_code", not "c") act as inline instructions.

intuition.analogy: JSON mode is a customs officer who checks the form is filled in ink — not that the answers are right.
paragraphs: The officer (JSON mode) verifies the paperwork is formally correct: right paper, right pen, parseable. They do not check that the declared value matches the goods, that every required box is ticked, or that the tariff code actually exists in the table.

Your validator is the second officer who checks the content against the rulebook (the schema) — and the repair loop is sending the form back with sticky notes saying exactly which boxes are wrong. A form sent back with precise notes comes back fixed; a form sent back saying "do better" comes back different, not better.

technical: Provider mechanics: chat APIs offer a JSON/response-format mode; stricter schema-guided modes constrain generation to a supplied JSON Schema. The stricter the mode, the more syntax is guaranteed — but field semantics (did it pick the RIGHT enum?) remain your responsibility.

Validation: define the schema in code. In Python, pydantic parses and coerces or raises per-field errors; in TypeScript, zod does the same. These error messages are gold — they are exactly what you feed into the repair prompt.

The repair loop: catch validation errors, format them verbatim ("year: expected number, received null"), instruct "fix ONLY these errors", re-validate. Bound retries (commonly 3) and define the terminal failure path: raise, log, or queue for human review — never silently drop.

Schema design rules that measurably reduce failures: use enums for any closed set; make genuinely unknown fields optional and omitted (null is a value the model will happily invent); prefer flat structures; keep one concept per field; and give the model an out ("if not stated in the input, omit") to discourage hallucination.

Testing: a fixed set of messy inputs, run through the pipeline, with first-pass and post-repair success rates recorded. You will build this into a full eval harness in Phase 4; the seed of it is a for-loop with counters.
deeper: How can syntax be guaranteed at all? Constrained decoding: at each generation step the sampler masks tokens that would violate the grammar (here: the JSON syntax or schema), so invalid sequences are never sampled. This is why schema-guided modes can promise valid JSON without post-processing.

The same machinery explains the limit: constraints operate on form, not meaning. The sampler can be forced to emit a string in the year field — it cannot be forced to emit the correct year. Truth remains a property of your prompt, your data, and your evals.
realWorld: Extraction pipelines (invoices, postings, tickets) — the most-shipped industrial LLM feature, and precisely this pattern: schema, validate, repair, measure.
Agent tool arguments: every tool call is structured output; wrong types or invented enum values are how agents crash, which is why Phase 2 feeds directly into Phase 6.
Evals: your Phase 4 golden sets consume schema-validated records — an eval harness over unvalidated prose measures nothing.

projects.title: API Insight Tracker
projects.problem: Public APIs give raw data; nobody has the trend. Track any public API (weather, crypto, GitHub stars) over time and surface the insight.
projects.evaluation: Unit tests on parsers with recorded API fixtures; integration test on a local SQLite; deterministic report snapshot test.

projects.title: Sentiment Analysis, Done Rigorously
projects.problem: Rebuild your social-media sentiment project with defensible methodology: cross-validation, a beaten baseline, calibrated metrics, and honest error analysis.
projects.evaluation: Grouped/times-aware cross-validation; confidence intervals via bootstrap; ablation table; train-serve skew check.

projects.title: Tool-Using Assistant
projects.problem: A CLI/web assistant that answers real questions using 3+ tools (weather, notes, calculator/search) — and never returns invalid JSON.
projects.evaluation: 30-prompt tool-selection suite in CI; schema-validity fuzz (500 sampled outputs); chaos tests with injected 429/500.

projects.title: Cited Document Q&A
projects.problem: "Ask my documents" apps hallucinate. Build one where every claim links to its source and quality is measured, not asserted.
projects.evaluation: Golden Q&A set; retrieval hit-rate@5 and MRR; faithfulness scoring (LLM-as-judge, spot-checked by hand); adversarial set for refusal.

projects.title: Capstone: Secure Deployed Agent
projects.problem: An agent that researches a topic and drafts an external action (email/report), requires human approval before acting, and runs as a hardened public service.
projects.evaluation: Task-success eval on 20 scenarios; injection red-team suite (must resist 10/10); load test within cost budget; tracing on every run.

projects.title: Eval-Backed Prompt Library
projects.problem: Teams hoard prompts in chat histories and notes files where they rot. You will build the alternative: a public, versioned library of prompt patterns where every entry ships with an automated eval suite, a changelog, and an honest "when not to use this" section.
projects.evaluation: Score each pattern on a golden set in CI (exact match or calibrated judge). Track pass rate per pattern over time; a release is shippable only when all patterns are green on their frozen golden sets.

projects.title: Production Extraction Service
projects.problem: Free-text data is locked in emails, PDFs, and posts. You will build the service that unlocks it: a schema-validated extraction API with a repair loop, honest error rates, and a cost model — the single most-shipped LLM feature, done properly.
projects.evaluation: Per-field precision and recall against a hand-labeled gold set, before and after repair. Cost and p95 latency per document. Terminal-failure behavior verified with adversarial inputs.

projects.title: Injection-Resistant RAG Assistant
projects.problem: Assistants that read retrieved content are assistants that execute strangers instructions. You will build a grounded Q&A assistant over a document set, then attack it yourself and engineer the layered defenses that keep it useful — with a red-team report proving what works.
projects.evaluation: Attack break rate per defense layer on a fixed suite of at least ten payloads. Answer quality held constant on your Phase-3 25-question benchmark (defenses must not destroy usefulness).

projects.title: Prompt Eval & Regression Harness
projects.problem: Prompts are edited constantly and tested never. You will build the harness that makes every prompt change an experiment: versioned prompts, a golden set, automated scoring with a calibrated judge, and a merge gate that blocks regressions.
projects.evaluation: Pass rate per prompt version on the frozen golden set; judge agreement rate against hand labels; CI run gating a planted bad edit.

projects.title: Multi-Turn Context Compression Engine
projects.problem: Long conversations blow the context budget and drift: constraints set on turn 2 are forgotten by turn 40. You will build the engine that keeps a multi-turn assistant coherent and cheap: rolling summaries, explicit constraint carry-over, and a hard token budget with graceful degradation.
projects.evaluation: Constraint retention rate across 50-turn conversations (programmatic checks), p95 per-turn latency, total token spend with vs without compression.
